issues.issue: "the Business" is defined only as "jointly developing Spanish language and bilingual print and media business", a boundary-less description that must nevertheless carry the weight of the noncompetition covenant later in paragraph 2. Two sides could reasonably differ on whether a given media or advertising activity falls inside it.

LSB is made responsible for "managing the day-to-day operations", including hiring, yet the immediately following sentence of paragraph 1 requires that "all expenditures must be done with the concurrence of DMSA" and paragraph 4 bars any member from incurring costs except per the approved budget. The scope of her operational authority cannot be fixed without reconciling those provisions.

The capital obligation is measured only by "an amount that DMSA deems appropriate" and the parenthetical lets DMSA count its own travel, legal, accounting and internal "labor of management and staff" as contributed capital. Both the existence of any minimum obligation and what may be booked as capital (and later repaid ahead of members under paragraph 4) are open to competing readings.

Distribution is left to what "the board decides to distribute", which sits against the mandatory annual tax distribution in the next sentence and the mandatory waterfall in paragraph 4. Whether the board's discretion is unfettered or subject to those provisions is contestable.

This makes the annual tax distribution mandatory ("shall distribute each year at least enough cash"), but paragraph 4 places the identical tax distribution third in a waterfall, behind reimbursement of out-of-pocket costs and repayment of DMSA's initial capital. The two cannot both be applied when client receipts are exhausted at the earlier tiers.

The undertaking to "jointly pursue the Business" through the LLC is immediately undercut by the following sentences allowing DMSA and its principals to retain and originate media, advertising contracts and clients for their own benefit whether or not similar to the LLC's Business. Whether the joint-pursuit covenant retains any operative content is exactly the sort of whole-instrument tension a court must resolve.

The carve-out for interests "that are not and will not be part of the LLC's business, whether similar to the LLC's Business or not" cannot be squared with the preceding covenant that the parties "shall through the LLC jointly pursue the Business". Which sentence governs when DMSA takes a Spanish-language media opportunity is genuinely open.

The enumeration "business, advertising contracts, marketing contracts, or any other contracts" ends in an open catch-all whose reach against the listed specifics is uncertain (ejusdem generis). It is unclear whether "any other contracts" sweeps in every commercial opportunity or only contracts of the enumerated advertising/marketing kind.

The disclaimer of "any obligation" to originate business for the LLC stands against the next sentence, in which DMSA "does agree that it intends to use diligent efforts to direct appropriate business to the Company". Whether DMSA owes anything at all turns on reconciling the two.

The right to "retain existing and originate new media opportunities, advertising contracts and clients for its own benefit" is difficult to reconcile with the paragraph 2 covenant to jointly pursue the Business through the LLC and with the confidentiality of client lists in paragraph 5. A court would have to decide which prevails when the same client is pursued.
